rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all 10 compounds, locate their elution window, and identify the limiting peak pairs. A moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen the gradient while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to test whether the two limiting pairs respond to slope. The current last-peak time leaves room to improve resolution without exceeding 10 minutes.

The limiting pair improved strongly with a shallower gradient. Narrowing the solvent window further reduces slope, while raising the starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Further narrow the gradient window to push the remaining limiting pair above R = 1.5. Raising phi0 should offset much of the added retention from the shallower slope, targeting full resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.
Injection 4 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shift the gradient window upward at unchanged slope to test whether all peaks can elute sooner while preserving full resolution.

Return to the fully resolved solvent program and raise temperature by 5 °C to test a shorter separation. This isolates temperature selectivity at the limiting pair while keeping injection 4 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether the limiting pair separates again after a temperature-driven elution-order reversal, potentially giving a faster fully resolved method. Keep the solvent program fixed to isolate temperature effects and check for new limiting pairs.

Slightly lengthen the gradient to improve the new limiting pair at 55 °C while checking that the other close pair remains resolved. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves room for this adjustment without a time penalty.

Use a gradient slope between injections 7 and 8 to target full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 8. Both close pairs are expected to remain above R = 1.5, though the margin will be modest.

Test a steeper, shorter gradient with a lower starting organic fraction to improve initial retention and potentially preserve separation of the early limiting pair. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Shorten injection 10's gradient by two minutes to seek an earlier last peak while retaining maximum CRF. The early close pair has some resolution margin, and the later limiting pair has tended to improve with steeper gradients at 55 °C.

Reduce the slope slightly relative to injection 11 to recover resolution of the early limiting pair. This intermediate slope should target full resolution with the last peak around 7.8 minutes, faster than injection 10.

Explore a faster, hotter gradient to test whether the early limiting pair separates after an elution-order reversal. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if this introduces new overlaps.

Test a substantially steeper gradient at 60 °C to push the early close pair farther apart on the reversed-order branch. This explores a much shorter separation while checking whether compression creates other unresolved pairs.

Explore low-temperature selectivity with a broad, fast gradient, since the hotter, steeper methods introduced persistent overlaps. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention, while this run tests whether a different elution order permits a shorter fully resolved separation.

Return to the promising 55 °C region and lower the starting organic fraction to test whether improved early selectivity supports a steeper gradient. This targets a slightly faster fully resolved separation than injection 12, with both central close pairs requiring verification.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with an intermediate steep slope at 60 °C to seek better separation on the reversed-order branch without excessive compression. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shift selectivity of the unresolved central pair, while reducing the slope to protect its neighboring separation. Check the first two peaks carefully because the stronger starting solvent may compromise their retention and resolution.

Test intermediate low-temperature selectivity with a relatively fast gradient, since 25 °C caused extensive overlap but 40 °C was much better. This checks another route to a shorter fully resolved method while retaining injection 16 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score result.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 16 to test the speed limit of the best-performing 55 °C separation. This may shorten the last-peak time, but the two central close pairs have little resolution margin and must be checked.

Test 30 °C for a selectivity window between the extensive co-elution at 25 °C and the different overlaps at 35 °C. The broad gradient should keep the run below the time-penalty threshold while checking whether this temperature offers another fully resolved solution.

Test the remaining intermediate temperature with a fast gradient to check for favorable selectivity after the central peaks reorder. Injection 16 already achieves the maximum CRF, so this is an exploratory attempt to shorten the fully resolved separation.

Use a slope between injections 16 and 20 to target a slightly shorter separation than injection 16 while retaining full resolution. Interpolation suggests both limiting pairs will remain just above R = 1.5.

Test a compromise between injection 12's speed and injection 8's larger resolution margin. The slope of 0.0607 organic fraction per minute should preserve full resolution with the last peak near 8.2 minutes.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 9 to seek an earlier last peak while retaining full resolution; interpolation predicts the limiting resolution near 1.56. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.
